title: Minimum Number of Arrows to Burst Balloons
description: Find the minimum arrows needed to burst all overlapping balloon intervals, using a greedy sort-by-end strategy.

sections.title: Minimum Number of Arrows to Burst Balloons

content.title: Minimum Number of Arrows to Burst Balloons

blocks.text: Balloons are represented as intervals points[i] = [xstart, xend]. An arrow shot at position x bursts every balloon whose interval contains x. Return the minimum number of arrows needed to burst all balloons.

blocks.caption: Sorting by end coordinate lets a single greedy arrow burst every balloon it can, before moving to the next.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Field","Details"],"rows":[["Input","points[][] (each [xstart, xend], intervals may overlap)"],["Arrow rule","One arrow at position x bursts every balloon with xstart <= x <= xend"],["Output","Minimum number of arrows to burst every balloon"]]}

blocks.text: This is a classic interval-scheduling greedy problem: sort by END coordinate, and greedily place each arrow at the earliest possible ending point among still-unburst balloons, since that maximizes how many OTHER overlapping balloons it can also burst.

blocks.title: Connection
blocks.text: This "sort by end, greedily pick the earliest-ending compatible choice" technique is the same one behind classic activity-selection and interval-scheduling problems.

Picture a row of overlapping balloon ranges along a number line. Shooting an arrow at the END of the earliest-ending balloon guarantees it bursts that balloon, and also bursts every OTHER balloon whose range still overlaps that exact point, since their ranges must extend at least that far (having not yet ended) and start at or before it (since they overlap).

blocks.caption: An arrow at the earliest end point bursts every balloon still overlapping there.

items: Sort balloons by their end coordinate.
Shoot an arrow at the end of the first (earliest-ending) unburst balloon.
Skip every subsequent balloon whose start is at or before that arrow position, since they are already burst; the next balloon whose start is AFTER the arrow position needs a new arrow.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Balloon","Arrow position so far","Action"],"rows":[["[1,6]","none","shoot arrow at 6, arrowPos = 6"],["[2,8]","6","start 2 <= 6, already burst"],["[7,12]","6","start 7 > 6, shoot new arrow at 12, arrowPos = 12"],["[10,16]","12","start 10 <= 12, already burst"]]}

blocks.title: Answer
blocks.text: Only 2 arrows are needed (at positions 6 and 12), matching the expected output. The first arrow bursts both [1,6] and [2,8]; the second bursts both [7,12] and [10,16].

A brute-force approach could try shooting an arrow at each unburst balloon's end, marking every other overlapping balloon as burst, and repeating until all are burst, scanning the full list each time. This is correct but checks every pair of balloons.

Sorting by end coordinate lets a single linear pass make the greedy choice directly: since balloons are processed in order of increasing end, the current arrow position (the end of the first unburst balloon in this order) is guaranteed to be the best possible choice, maximizing how many later balloons it can also burst before a new arrow is ever needed.
For each still-unburst balloon in original order, shoot an arrow at its end coordinate and mark every overlapping balloon (checked against all others) as burst.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Metric","Value","Why"],"rows":[["Time","O(n^2)","Each arrow shot potentially rescans all n balloons"],["Space","O(n)","The burst-tracking array"]]}

blocks.title: Bottleneck
blocks.text: Rescanning all balloons for every arrow is unnecessary once sorting by end coordinate lets a single linear pass make the correct greedy decision at each step.

Sort balloons by end coordinate. Track the current arrow position, initialized to the first balloon's end. Walk through the remaining balloons in order; if a balloon's start exceeds the current arrow position, it is not burst yet, so shoot a new arrow at its end and update the arrow position.

items: Sort by end coordinate, O(n log n).
Initialize arrows = 1, arrowPos = first balloon's end.
For each subsequent balloon, if its start exceeds arrowPos, increment arrows and update arrowPos to its end.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Approach","Time","Space"],"rows":[["Brute Force, rescan on each arrow","O(n^2)","O(n)"],["Optimized, sort by end + greedy sweep","O(n log n)","O(n)"]]}

items: "Minimum points to cover all overlapping intervals" is solved by sorting by end coordinate and greedily placing each point at the earliest possible end.
Sorting by END (not start) is what guarantees the greedy choice at each step is optimal, since it maximizes how many later intervals the current point can also cover.
This exact greedy pattern is the classic interval point-covering technique, reused across many overlapping-interval problems.

blocks.text: Minimum Number of Arrows to Burst Balloons is solved by sorting balloons by end coordinate and greedily shooting each arrow at the earliest unburst balloon's end, since that choice bursts the maximum possible number of overlapping later balloons before a new arrow is needed, giving an O(n log n) solution.
